note: The seeds WP19 G3's rolling freeze is checked with, and the one place their names are spelled.

release.yml attaches an asset called nish-<version>-<asset>.tar.gz, builds its `binaries` matrix from this file, and ci.yml's `seeds` job looks for exactly that name. Every one of those reads it from here rather than stating it, because a contract each side writes out separately is two strings that agree until one of them is edited.

`triple` is the canonical target triple self/target.ts accepts, and `asset` is that triple with the vendor and the ABI dropped: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -> x86_64-linux, aarch64-apple-darwin -> aarch64-darwin. That derivation is the whole rule, and tests/run.js checks both halves against the compiler's own table, so a row that invents a platform the compiler cannot target fails there rather than on a release day.

`attachedSince` is the first version whose release attaches this seed, and it is a VERSION rather than a boolean because the boolean could not be flipped. A release that carries no seed for a target already due FAILS the `seeds` job: a host that could have checked the rolling freeze and did not is a broken gate. A target not yet due gets no bootstrap row at all -- an absent row says the freeze was not checked there, where a green row with a warning inside it would say it was. .github/seed-due.sh is the one place the comparison is made.

The boolean this replaced deadlocked the release it was waiting for. `attached: true` means "release.yml builds this today", which is a statement about the workflow; `seeds` reads it as a statement about the last *release*, which is a past event that cannot grow an asset. So the commit that taught release.yml to build the darwin pair could not also mark them attached: v0.2.0 does not carry them, `seeds` would go red, and release.yml's `release` job is `needs: ci` -- the release that would attach them could not be cut, and the flag could not be cleared until it was. A version says which releases the claim is about, so the two land together.

`host` is `uname -s`-`uname -m` on that platform, and release.yml's `binaries` job refuses to stamp the asset name into a tarball built on a machine that prints something else -- the last guard between a mislabelled asset and a user. `runner` is the GitHub-hosted label that provides that host, and it is executable configuration: release.yml's matrix and ci.yml's `bootstrap` both `runs-on` it. tests/run.js derives `host` from `triple` and checks `runner` against a denylist of labels GitHub has retired, because `macos-13` stood in this file after the last Intel image under that name was retired, and the day a release attached x86_64-darwin its bootstrap row would have had nowhere to run.

WHY ALL THREE NEW TARGETS ARE 0.4.0, AND WHAT EACH WAITED ON. None of the three had ever run here, and the rule two notes down says to exercise a platform's rows before its version arrives. All three obeyed it: they were exercised on 2026-09-19, on the hardware their rows name, and all three pass. What they were waiting FOR differed, and the difference is why one of them was green on the first try and the pair took four runs. `aarch64-linux` waited on the exercising and nothing else: it is ELF, so the Mach-O comparison below never applied to it, and one green throwaway run was the whole of what it needed -- which made it the natural first row to attach, and it went green immediately and stayed green. The darwin pair waited on the exercising AND on the ld64 measurement, and that measurement did turn up work before a row could pass, which is the note below.

WHAT THE DARWIN PAIR'S MEASUREMENT FOUND. `attachedSince` decides whether a target is BUILT, not only whether it is carried: release.yml's `targets` job runs .github/seed-due.sh for the version being released and its `binaries` matrix is that answer, so a target not yet due gets no matrix row at all. `scripts/bootstrap.sh --verify` asserts `stage3 == stage2`, which did not hold on Mach-O, and `release` is `needs: binaries`, deliberately, so a row failing as UNATTRIBUTED stops the release -- which is what both darwin rows did on the first exercising run. The measurement that run existed to make says why: LC_UUID, sixteen bytes at 0x468 and nothing else on x86_64-darwin, plus on aarch64-darwin the one code-directory slot that hashes the page it sits on, because ld64 ad-hoc signs arm64. Neither one-liner the old header proposed was the answer. -Wl,-no_uuid is unavailable: dyld on arm64 refuses an image with no LC_UUID (`missing LC_UUID load command`, then SIGABRT), so the compiler links and will not start. What settled it was a third measurement: the UUID is stable across two links to one output path and differs on a link to another, so bootstrap.sh building stage2 and stage3 at two paths gave two UUIDs to two compilers that agreed about every other byte. The output path is the leading explanation and not the only one that probe leaves standing -- its two same-path links ran first and it never went back to the first path, so path-identity and invocation-order are confounded, and a fourth link back to the first path is what would separate them. It was not run, and the remedy does not rest on it: both stages are linked at one path now, the comparison is still a raw cmp, and run 4 measured both rows green end to end through the bootstrap, the tarball check and the smoke test. scripts/verify-binaries.sh's header carries the measurement with its offsets.

BEFORE ADDING A PLATFORM, EXERCISE ITS ROWS ONCE. ci.yml's `bootstrap` job takes its matrix from the seeds a release ATTACHES, not from attachedSince (seed-matrix.sh checks presence first), so the release that first carries a seed gives that platform a bootstrap row on every push and every pull request from then on -- npm ci, an LLVM install, bootstrap.sh --verify and the CLI contract, on hardware none of it has run on. If that row is red, `ci` is red repo-wide and `release` is `needs: ci`. Rolling attachedSince back does NOT clear it, because the asset is already attached and presence is what makes the row: the only remedies are to fix the row or to delete the asset from the release. This rule has no exceptions in this file, deliberately: a rule the file states and the rows beneath it break is weaker than no rule, because the next person cites the exception rather than the rule. `aarch64-linux` was briefly 0.3.0 on the ELF argument -- sound about the Mach-O hazard, and about the wrong hazard: the half that is not fail-safe triggers on the row SUCCEEDING and being attached, not on it failing, and the release it would have landed on publishes to npm and is merged by a person who cannot be handed a debug cycle at that moment.

HOW TO EXERCISE A PLATFORM'S ROWS, given that the two obvious ways are closed. release.yml cannot be dispatched at a branch -- `targets` exits 1 unless GITHUB_REF_TYPE is a tag and the tag equals package.json's version -- so a dispatch can only ever be aimed at the exact version being released, and a temporary matrix entry in release.yml cannot be reached either. What does work is a throwaway workflow on a branch: `on: workflow_dispatch`, one job `runs-on:` the label in question, and the steps of release.yml's `binaries` job down to the smoke test, with no upload. It is deleted once it has been green, and it leaves nothing permanent in a workflow whose failures are expensive. Making release.yml itself capable of a dry run -- a version input on workflow_dispatch that builds without attaching -- would be the principled fix and is deliberately not done here: it adds a path to the publishing workflow that has itself never run, which is the thing this note is about.

THAT IS WHAT WAS DONE FOR THE THREE ROWS ABOVE, with one correction to the recipe. The throwaway took its matrix from .github/seed-due.sh's answer inverted -- every row the current version is NOT due, which is exactly the set no release has carried -- so it named no platform of its own, and it ran all three at once with `fail-fast: false` so a red row would name itself rather than hide behind whichever failed first. The correction: `workflow_dispatch` needs `actions: write`, and a token holding `actions: read` gets a 403 from the dispatch API however well-formed the workflow is. A branch-scoped `push:` trigger runs the same jobs on the same hardware with the same steps, needs no extra permission, and goes away with the branch, so the throwaway is as throwaway as before. Carry both next time: the dispatch for whoever has the permission, the push for whoever does not. docs/wp10-ci.md#ci-matrix has the four runs it took and what each row did in each.

WHICH RELEASE nish-cmp CAN COMPARE AGAINST, AND WHY IT IS NOT THE FIRST. `cmpSince` is to WP19 G2.1 what `attachedSince` is to G3, and it is a version for the identical reason: a release already published cannot grow a file. tests/nish-cmp.js compiles the corpus with the last released compiler and with the one HEAD builds and requires every byte to match, so it is only meaningful against a seed that can compile the corpus -- and the seeds 0.1.1 through 0.4.0 carry cannot. Every one of them was staged as bin + runtime + scripts and no std/, so the compiler they contain answers any `import { trim } from "nish/text"` with ``Module `nish/text` is not part of the standard library (it has: json, testing, text)``, naming the module it refuses because the list in that sentence is static and the file is what is absent. Against such a seed nish-cmp reports two corpus programs on which the candidate is simply right -- tests/link/std_bare_specifier and tests/link/std_package_scope, the two that reach the library by its package specifier rather than by a path, which is the only form that goes through the compiler package root the staging broke.

SO THE GATE WAITS FOR A SEED RATHER THAN ALLOWLISTING THE DIFFERENCE. Declaring those two programs in the tool's DECLARED list was the other way, and it is worse twice over: the difference is the seed's defect and not a decided change of output, and the mechanism cannot be satisfied anyway -- DECLARED requires the words to appear in CHANGELOG.md, and CHANGELOG.md is generated at release time with [Unreleased] deliberately empty, so no declaration can be green between releases. An absent row says no comparison happened; a green one with an allowlist inside it would say a comparison happened and passed. docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md §A5 is what the second costs. Move this to the version being released only when that release's binaries job stages std/, which release.yml has done since 2026-09-20.

WHY IT IS 0.6.0 AND NOT 0.5.0, WHICH IS A SECOND REASON ON TOP OF THE FIRST. The paragraph above is about a FLOOR: no release before 0.5.0 can be compared against at all, because none of them ships std/, and that is permanent. This field read 0.6.0 for a different and temporary reason: WP30 (docs/wp30-bytes-interop.md) makes the unsigned widths cross as typed arrays, which is a DECIDED change to generated output, so HEAD and the 0.5.0 seed disagree about eleven files on purpose -- eight loaders whose one shared line carries a corrected indefinite article, and three sidecars of bench/scan.ts where 0.5.0 declines a `u8[]` that HEAD exports. Every one of those is the package working.

AND WHY THE OTHER THREE WAYS OUT ARE WORSE. The note above already rules out DECLARED: it cannot be green between releases, by construction. Reverting the article fix would cut eleven differences to three and reach green on none of them, because the three ARE the feature. Keeping bench/scan.ts out of the corpus would go green by arranging for the comparison not to see the change, which is the sentence above about an allowlist, wearing a different hat. What is left is an absent row, which is this field's own mechanism and says the true thing: no comparison happened. The cost is real and belongs here rather than in a commit message -- G2.1 is dark for every change until 0.6.0 ships, so an UNintended output change in that window is caught by nothing. It is the narrowest window the field can express, because the next release carries WP30 and the gate comes back with no edit to ci.yml.

THE DEADLOCK THIS AVOIDS, WHICH IS THE SAME ONE attachedSince's note describes. release.yml's release job is `needs: ci`, so a red CI is a release that cannot be cut. Merging WP30 with nish-cmp red would leave main red, and a red main cuts no release, and only a release carrying WP30 makes the difference go away: the gate would be waiting for a seed that the gate itself prevents. Moving the field is what breaks that, and it is why the move lands in the SAME pull request as the output change rather than after it.

AND WHY IT IS 0.8.0 NOW, WHICH IS THE SAME REASON AGAIN. WP18 G6 (docs/wp18-generics.md §15.6) accepts a constrained type parameter, `<T extends Shape>`, and that is a DECIDED change of output of the same kind as WP30's: six corpus programs that the 0.6.0 seed refuses by syntax (``a constrained type parameter (`T extends ...`) is not supported yet``) and HEAD compiles -- tests/cases/gen_constraint, gen_constraint_class, gen_constraint_generic_bound and gen_constraint_method, docs/cookbook/gen_constraint.ts, and tests/link/generic_constraint_import/main.ts. Every other program of the corpus agreed byte for byte on the run that found them. The ways out are the ones the paragraphs above already weighed: DECLARED cannot be green between releases, keeping the six out of the corpus would hide the construct from the gate that exists to see it, and merging G6 with nish-cmp red would leave main red, which cuts no release -- the deadlock above, again. So the field moves to the first release that carries G6, and in the same pull request. That is 0.8.0 rather than 0.7.1: G6 is a `feat!`, scripts/changelog-gen.mjs moves the minor for a breaking change before 1.0, and v0.7.0 was tagged before G6 merged, so the 0.7.0 seed would refuse the same six programs if its release is published first. The dark window is the one WP30's paragraph priced, and longer: until 0.8.0 ships, G2.1 and the `fuzz.js --stage1` comparison that shares its seed compare nothing, so an UNintended output change in that window is caught by the goldens and the bootstrap and by nothing else. The first release carrying G6 brings the row back with no edit to ci.yml, and this paragraph becomes history the way the two above it are.
